title: Commission agreements for property agents: a checklist for Pakistan
description: A checklist for agreeing commission with property agents and partners in Pakistan: rates, timing, split rules and cancellations written down clearly.
faq: What should a commission agreement cover?
Who earns commission, how it is calculated, when it is paid, how it is shared and what happens if the sale is cancelled.
Does the agreement need to be formal?
It should at least be written and signed by both sides. Check with a qualified adviser for legal requirements.
body: Commission disputes often come from verbal promises. Writing the terms down before the deal protects everyone. This is general guidance, not legal advice.
# What to write down
* Names of the parties and the property or project.
* The commission rate or fixed amount.
* What it is calculated on, such as the sale price or the amount received.
* When it is paid: on booking, on down payment or as instalments arrive.
* How it is split between several agents.
* What happens if the buyer cancels or defaults.
# Keep a clear record
Record each commission as earned, approved and paid. Everyone should be able to see the status.
# Review regularly
Check your standard terms once a year. If you change them, apply the new terms only to new deals and tell people clearly.

title: Construction project management checklist for Pakistani contractors
description: A checklist for managing a construction project in Pakistan: scope, budget, schedule, purchases, labour, progress and billing from start to handover.
faq: What should a contractor track on every project?
Budget against actual cost, purchases, labour, subcontractor payments, progress and client billing.
How often should progress be reviewed?
Weekly at least, with a short daily site report.
body: Most overruns come from small things that were not tracked: an extra purchase, an unpaid advance, a change that was never priced. A simple checklist keeps them visible.
# Before starting
* Written scope and the agreed price or BOQ.
* A budget by stage or cost head.
* A schedule with key dates.
* Names and contacts for suppliers and subcontractors.
# During the project
* Daily site report: work done, labour present, materials received.
* Purchase orders for every material order.
* Record advances and payments to subcontractors.
* Track variations and get them approved in writing.
# Billing and handover
Bill the client by measured progress and keep measurement records. At handover, keep a final account showing budget, actual cost and what was billed.
# Review every week
Compare spend with progress. If cost is rising faster than work done, find out why while it can still be fixed.

title: The daily site progress report: what to record and why
description: What a daily construction progress report should contain in Pakistan: work done, labour, materials, equipment, delays and photos, and how to use it.
faq: What is a daily site report?
A short record of what happened on site that day: work completed, workers present, materials received, issues and photos.
Who should write it?
The site engineer or supervisor, on the same day.
body: The daily report is the cheapest control tool on a project. It takes ten minutes and settles many later arguments about what was done and when.
# What to include
* Date, weather if it affected work, and the area worked on.
* Work completed and its approximate quantity.
* Number of workers by trade.
* Materials received and used.
* Equipment on site.
* Delays, problems and instructions received.
* A few dated photos.
# How it helps
* It supports your progress bill with evidence.
* It shows delays and their cause when the client disputes the schedule.
* It helps you compare labour on site with work completed.
# Keep it consistent
Use the same format every day and store reports in one place, so a report from three months ago can be found in a minute.

title: Construction labour attendance and wages: keeping fair records
description: How to keep labour attendance and wage records on a construction site in Pakistan: daily attendance, rates, advances, deductions and payment proof.
faq: What should labour records include?
Name, trade, daily rate or piece rate, days worked, advances, deductions and payment date.
Why record advances carefully?
Advances are easy to forget and are a common cause of wage disputes.
body: Labour is a large part of site cost and a frequent source of disputes. Clear records protect both the contractor and the worker.
# Daily attendance
Mark attendance each day, by name and trade. Have the supervisor sign or confirm it so there is an agreed record.
# Rates and calculations
* Record the agreed daily or piece rate for each worker or gang.
* Calculate wages from the attendance record, not from memory.
* Show the calculation so the worker can check it.
# Advances and deductions
Write every advance with its date and reason, and deduct it according to the agreed plan. Show the balance on the pay slip.
# Pay and record
Record the date and mode of each payment and get an acknowledgement. At the end of the project you will have a complete labour cost per site.

title: Construction site store management: stop material wastage and theft
description: How to manage a construction site store in Pakistan: receiving, issuing, stock counts and reconciling purchases against use to cut wastage.
faq: How do I reduce material loss on site?
Record every receipt and issue, count stock regularly and compare use against work done.
Who should control the store?
One responsible person, with a second person checking regularly.
body: Materials are often the biggest cost on a construction project, and a poorly controlled store leaks money quietly. A simple routine closes most gaps.
# Receive properly
* Check every delivery against the purchase order.
* Count or weigh the goods and note any shortage or damage.
* Record the receipt with date, supplier and quantity.
# Issue with a record
Record what leaves the store, who took it and for which work. Issue slips signed by the supervisor make use traceable.
# Count and reconcile
Count the main items weekly. Compare stock with the record; investigate differences quickly while memories are fresh.
# Compare use with progress
If cement or steel used is much higher than the work completed would suggest, look for wastage, theft or unrecorded changes.

title: Supplier ledgers for contractors: pay on time and avoid disputes
description: How contractors in Pakistan can keep supplier ledgers: purchases, deliveries, payments and balances so that accounts match at month end.
faq: What is a supplier ledger?
A running account for each supplier showing purchases, payments and the balance owed.
How often should I reconcile with suppliers?
Monthly at least, and before any large payment.
body: Suppliers extend credit to contractors they trust. A clear ledger keeps that trust and avoids month-end arguments about what was ordered and delivered.
# What each ledger should show
* Date, purchase order and delivery note number.
* Amount of each purchase.
* Payments made, with date and mode.
* Running balance.
# Match three documents
Before paying, match the purchase order, the delivery record and the supplier invoice. If they do not agree, resolve it first.
# Reconcile monthly
Send each main supplier a statement and ask them to confirm. Differences are far easier to solve when they are a month old than when they are a year old.
# Plan payments
Use the ledger to see what is due this week and next, so you can plan cash instead of reacting to phone calls.

title: Construction cash flow in Pakistan: why profitable projects still run short of money
description: Why construction projects in Pakistan run short of cash even when profitable, and how to plan billing, payments and advances to keep work moving.
faq: Why do profitable projects have cash problems?
Costs are paid up front while client payments arrive later, so timing, not profit, creates the gap.
How can I improve cash flow?
Bill promptly on measured progress, plan payments to suppliers and track what is owed by the client.
body: A project can make a profit on paper and still leave you short of money every month. The reason is timing: you pay for labour and materials now and the client pays later.
# Know your cycle
Work out how many days pass between spending money and receiving it from the client. The longer the gap, the more cash you need to carry.
# Bill on time
* Measure progress regularly and submit the bill straight away.
* Keep measurement sheets ready to support the bill.
* Follow up unpaid bills with dates and names.
# Plan outgoing payments
List what is due to suppliers, labour and subcontractors for the next four weeks and compare with expected receipts.
# Watch retention and advances
Track retention amounts and advances separately so you know when money is due back to you.

title: Construction ERP kya hai? Contractors ke liye asan wazahat
description: Construction ERP kya hota hai, contractors ko kyun chahiye aur kaun se kaam ek jagah ho sakte hain: BOQ, purchase, labour aur billing.
faq: Construction ERP kya hota hai?
Ek software jo budget, purchase, labour, store, subcontractor aur client billing ek jagah rakhta hai.
Kya chhote contractor ke liye bhi faida hai?
Haan, agar aap ke paas kai sites ya bohat se suppliers hain to records ek jagah hone se hisab asan hota hai.
body: ERP ka matlab hai ek aisa system jahan business ke alag alag kaam ek doosre se jude hote hain. Construction mein yeh budget, purchase, labour, store aur billing hote hain.
# Contractors ke aam masail
* Budget Excel mein hota hai aur kharcha kisi aur register mein.
* Supplier ka hisab mahine ke end par match nahi hota.
* Labour ki advance bhool jati hai.
* Client ko bill banane mein der hoti hai.
# ERP kya karta hai
* BOQ aur budget banata hai.
* Purchase order aur store ka record rakhta hai.
* Labour aur subcontractor ki payment ka hisab rakhta hai.
* Progress ke hisab se client bill banata hai.
# Shuru kaise karein
Pehle ek project ka BOQ aur budget daalein, phir purchases aur labour record karna shuru karein. Ek hi project se seekhna sab se asan hai.

title: Running several property offices: keeping branches, agents and accounts organised
description: How a property business in Pakistan can run several offices: shared lead records, agent access, branch-wise accounts and consistent receipts.
faq: What changes when you open a second office?
You can no longer see everything yourself, so you need shared records, clear roles and branch-wise reports.
Should every branch see all data?
No. Give staff access only to what their role needs.
body: Running one office, you can watch everything yourself. With two or three, problems hide in the gaps between them. Shared records and clear rules keep control.
# One system, not three notebooks
Keep leads, properties and payments in one system so the owner sees all branches. Duplicate records and double bookings become easier to catch.
# Branch-wise accounts
Record income and expenses by branch so you can see which office performs. Use the same receipt format everywhere.
# Roles and access
* Agents see their own leads and clients.
* Branch managers see their branch.
* Owners and accountants see all branches and reports.
# Common policies
Use the same commission rules, follow-up standards and document checklist in every office, and review them together regularly.

title: Seven reports every property business owner in Pakistan should check
description: Seven simple reports for property business owners in Pakistan: leads, visits, sales, collections, overdue instalments, commissions and cash position.
faq: How often should owners check reports?
Weekly for leads, visits and collections, and monthly for profit and commissions.
Do reports need special software?
No, but software makes them faster and more reliable than building them by hand.
body: Owners do not need dozens of reports. A few, checked regularly, show whether the business is healthy.
# The seven reports
* New leads by source.
* Site visits booked and held.
* Sales closed and their value.
* Payments collected against what was due.
* Overdue instalments by buyer and age.
* Commissions earned and paid.
* Cash position: money in, money out and balance.
# How to use them
Review leads and visits weekly with the team. Review collections and overdue instalments weekly with accounts. Review commissions and cash monthly.
# Look for trends
One week's number tells little. A fall over several weeks tells you where to look.
